name: Liskov Substitution Principle
intent: Make every subtype usable wherever its base type is expected, without the caller noticing: a subtype may do more than the contract promises, but never demand more from the caller or deliver less.
scenario: A client function works with a Bag of integers: it adds values, removes them and checks the size. Four subclasses are written by reusing the same list code: an honest one, one that ignores duplicates, one that rejects values up to zero and one that throws on every add. All four compile and are accepted wherever a Bag is expected. The same client then runs its five checks against each, and the same is done with a Rectangle and a Square.
problem: A type system checks that the method names and signatures match. It does not check what the methods promise. A subclass can satisfy the compiler and still break the callers, because it changes behaviour that the callers rely on: a method that used to accept any integer now throws, a size that used to grow now stays the same. The caller then needs an instanceof check or a special case for each subtype, and the abstraction has stopped abstracting. The usual cause is inheritance used to reuse code instead of to model a real is-a relationship in behaviour.

howItWorks.title: Write the contract down
howItWorks.text: A base type has a contract even if nobody wrote it: what a caller must provide (preconditions), what the method guarantees afterwards (postconditions) and what always holds about the object (invariants). For the Bag: add accepts any integer, afterwards contains is true and the size grew by one, and size always equals adds minus removes. Tests and comments are a good place to keep it.

howItWorks.title: A subtype may not demand more
howItWorks.text: A subtype can accept everything the base type accepts, and more, but it cannot narrow the inputs. PositiveBag rejects values up to zero, which the base type accepts, so a caller that passes -1 gets an exception it did not plan for. ReadOnlyBag is the extreme: it narrows the accepted inputs to nothing, because add always throws.

howItWorks.title: A subtype may not deliver less
howItWorks.text: A subtype can promise more than the base type, but not less. DedupBag keeps one copy of a repeated value, so after two adds the size is 1 and the guarantee that the size grew by one is gone. The classic Square that inherits Rectangle breaks a postcondition too: a caller that sets the width to 5 and the height to 4 expects an area of 20 and gets 16.

howItWorks.title: Run the client's checks against each subtype
howItWorks.text: The test of a substitute is behavioural: run the checks the client relies on against every subtype. The honest ListBag passes 5 of 5, DedupBag 3 of 5, PositiveBag 4 of 5 and ReadOnlyBag 0 of 5. Contract tests that every subtype must pass are the practical way to catch a violation before a caller does.

howItWorks.title: Fix it by changing the relationship, not the caller
howItWorks.text: If a type cannot keep the contract, it should not claim to be that type. A ReadOnlyView built by composition holds a list and offers only reading, so it is not a Bag and the writer client never receives it, while the clients that need only reading accept it. A Square that offers only an area can be used wherever a shape is wanted. Prefer composition and small interfaces over inheritance for reuse.

pros: Callers can rely on the base type without a check for each subtype
New subtypes can be added without breaking existing callers
Contract tests catch broken substitutes in the subtype's own build
Pushes designs toward small interfaces and composition
cons: The contract must be known and written down, which many codebases never do
Real-world hierarchies often have cases that do not fit a strict contract
Follows from behaviour, not from the types, so the compiler cannot check it
Keeping subtypes honest can mean more types or more composition than a quick inheritance would
whenToUse: Any code that accepts a base type or interface and must work with every subtype
Libraries and frameworks whose callers write their own subtypes
When a subclass overrides a method to throw, to do nothing or to ignore an argument
whenNotToUse: As a reason to avoid inheritance altogether: honest subtypes are fine
For code where the subtypes are never used through the base type, so no caller depends on the contract
As a purely formal check of signatures: the principle is about behaviour
pitfalls: Treating it as a compiler matter: a subtype that type-checks can still break every caller
A read-only list that throws on add, so callers need instanceof checks before writing
A Square that inherits Rectangle and changes both sides in each setter, so area calculations are wrong
A Bird base class with a fly method, and penguins that throw: the base type promised too much
Using inheritance to reuse code instead of to model a real is-a relationship in behaviour
Overriding a method to do nothing or to ignore an argument, which weakens the postcondition silently

roles.label: Client function
roles.description: Written against the base contract; runs the checks.

roles.label: Base type
roles.description: Defines the contract callers rely on.

roles.label: Honest subtype
roles.description: Keeps every promise of the base type.

roles.label: Breaking subtype
roles.description: Compiles, but changes behaviour the client relies on.

roles.label: Composed type
roles.description: Reuses code by holding it, without claiming to be the base type.

quiz.question: A ReadOnlyList extends List and throws when add is called. Code that takes a List calls add and crashes. Which statement is accurate?
options: The subclass is fine, because the compiler accepted it as a List.
The subclass breaks the contract: it strengthens the precondition of add to never.
The caller is at fault for calling add without checking the type first.
The problem is only the exception, and returning silently would be correct.
quiz.explanation: A List promises that add works. A subtype that rejects every add demands more than the base type, so callers cannot use it as a List. Passing the compiler is not the test, and silently ignoring add would weaken the postcondition instead.

quiz.question: A client sets a Rectangle's width to 5 and then its height to 4 and expects an area of 20. A Square subclass returns 16. What rule is broken?
options: The invariant that a rectangle has at least one side longer than the other.
The precondition that the width must be set before the height.
The principle that subclasses must have the same constructor as their parent.
The postcondition that setting one side leaves the other side unchanged.
quiz.explanation: The Rectangle contract says the setters change only their own side. A Square that changes both delivers less than the base type promised. The relationship holds in geometry but not in behaviour of mutable objects.

quiz.question: A team needs a collection that can be read but never written. Which design best follows the Liskov Substitution Principle?
options: Subclass the mutable list and override add to throw an error.
Subclass the mutable list and override add to do nothing.
A separate read-only type that wraps a list and offers only reading methods.
Subclass the mutable list and document that add must not be called.
quiz.explanation: A type that does not offer add makes no promise about it, so no client can be surprised. Throwing, ignoring or documenting the call all keep the claim that it is a mutable list while breaking the promise.
